newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity prices ease in quiet trade.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity prices ease in quiet trade.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures eased Tuesday in quiet trade with September taking over as the front month contract, industry sources said.

As of 1225 EDT, September Palo Verde (PV) was trading down 53 cents at $30.15 per megawatt hour (MWh) following exchanges at $30.05-30.75, while October was down 55 cents at the day's low of $23.15 after reaching as high as $23.40 per MWh.

September California Oregon Border (COB) was trading down five cents at the day's low of $22.90 after reaching as high as $23.20, while October was down five cents at the day's high of $21.70 following trade as low as $21.50 per MWh.
NYMEX said as of 1150 EDT an estimated total of 168 PV and 93 COB contracts had traded.
Next-day firm, peak physical prices were reported to have fallen, with PV pegged at $34.00-36.00 early Tuesday and COB at $17.25-17.75, market sources said.

In generation news, the 550 megawatt (MW) unit 3 at the Jim Bridger coal-fired power plant in Wyoming was expected to restart late Wednesday after being taken off line late Monday, sources familiar with the plant's operations said.
The unit was shut for replacement of a fan, and Bridger's other three 550 MW units were said to be operating normally.

Also, the 254 MW unit 1 at the Valmy coal-fired power plant in Nevada will likely be off line for a week after being shut late Monday due to a rotor problem, sources familiar with the plant's operations said. The plant's other 267 MW unit was said to be operating normally.

The 1,221 MW Palo Verde 2 nuclear power unit in Arizona began slowly coasting down to its September refueling outage. The unit was running at 98 percent early Tuesday, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission said in its daily status report.
The 750 MW Four Corners coal-fired unit 5 in New Mexico, shut earlier this month to repair a high pressure generator field, was planned to restart next week.
Damage to a fish ladder at the Bonneville Dam on the Columbia River in Oregon could reduce power output at the project by 200 MW for a month or two.

To clear space for future runoffs, the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation was scheduled last Sunday to begin releasing extra water and producing more electricity at its Hoover, Davis and Parker hydroelectric projects.
The Hoover hydropower plant in Nevada has a generating capacity of 1,037 MW, Davis in Arizona has a capacity of 240 MW, while Parker in California is 120 MW.

On Thursday, southbound transfer capability on the AC segment of the Pacific Intertie transmission system will be cut by 150 MW to 3,300 MW between 1000-1300 PDT due to maintenance on a 500 kilovolt section of the lines.
Final approval from the Western Systems Coordinating Council (WSCC) to increase the intertie's capacity to 6,900 MW from 6,300 is expected later this week.

The latest six to 10 day forecasts showed the West would experience seasonal to slightly cooler-than-seasonal readings regionwide with a monsoonal flow bringing above-normal precipitation in the mountainous areas.
As of 1225 EDT, NYMEX September Henry Hub natural gas was trading down 1.3 cents at $2.138 per million British thermal units.
COB open interest for July 28 fell 490 to 5,600 while PV open interest fell 98 to 5,552, NYMEX said.
